blogs.title: The Amylase Whisper: Cracking Hemorrhagic Pleural Effusions
blogs.description: Walk through a pragmatic approach to amylase-rich pleural effusions in children. Contrast pancreatopleural fistula (PPF) with other causes of elevated pleural amylase (esophageal perforation with salivary-type amylase, malignancy, and rare TB associations). Highlight the diagnostic clue of pleural fluid amylase ≥1000 IU/L suggesting PPF, why amylase isoenzyme typing (pancreatic vs salivary) matters, and how a simple add-on test can prevent weeks of misdirected pulmonary workups.

blogs.title: Imaging the Invisible Leak: CT, MRCP, and ERCP for Suspected PPF in Kids
blogs.description: Detail a stepwise imaging strategy when PPF is on the table. Summarize what each modality offers and its limitations: CT for complications and collections yet fistula visualization only ~33%–47%; MRCP sensitivity ~70%–80% for ductal anatomy and fistula path without radiation; ERCP as the therapeutic gold standard and definitive ductal map. Include when to escalate from CXR/bedside lung ultrasound to cross-sectional imaging, radiation considerations in pediatrics, and pearls from this case where a right paraesophageal tract to the pancreatic tail was identified.

blogs.title: Conservative First, Plan the Exit: Managing Pediatric Pancreatopleural Fistula
blogs.description: Outline a treatment ladder tailored to children: initial bowel rest, total parenteral nutrition, octreotide 10–40 µg/kg/day (case used 30 µg/kg/day), pancreatic enzyme replacement, and controlled pleural drainage. Set realistic expectations (pediatric conservative success ~12%) and define failure/time-to-escalate (2–3 weeks). Review the role and success of ERCP with transpapillary stenting (pediatric success ~100%; mixed-age long-term >90%), and when to proceed to surgery (distal pancreatectomy, Puestow, cystojejunostomy; ~93% success, <5% mortality).

blogs.title: The TB Trap: When ADA Misleads and Anchoring Hurts
blogs.description: Use this case to examine cognitive and diagnostic pitfalls in pediatric pleural effusion. Discuss why mildly elevated pleural ADA is nonspecific, how TB contact history can bias decisions, and the importance of integrating microbiologic testing (e.g., GeneXpert), cytology, and clinical context before starting antitubercular therapy. Provide practical ADA thresholds, emphasize pretest probability, and propose a checkpoint list to avoid anchoring when effusions are hemorrhagic and recurrent.

blogs.title: The Pulmonary Mask of Abdominal Disease: Think Trauma and Diaphragmatic Highways
blogs.description: Highlight how intra-abdominal processes present with dominant chest findings in kids. Review the anatomic routes pancreatic fluid uses to reach the pleura via the esophageal or aortic hiatus, explaining right- or bilateral-sided effusions. Stress meticulous history-taking for blunt abdominal trauma (including delayed disclosure) and why most pediatric PPFs initially appear as recurrent pleural effusions with minimal abdominal symptoms. Offer a short differential for other abdominal-to-thoracic masqueraders to keep on the radar.

blogs.title: Draining the Dilemma: Thoracentesis vs Chest Tube in High-Output Pediatric Effusions
blogs.description: Translate this case’s repeated 1-liter taps and subsequent intercostal drain into practice pearls. Cover indications for serial thoracentesis vs tube thoracostomy, ultrasound guidance, strategies to mitigate re-expansion pulmonary edema in children, handling hydropneumothorax, and how drainage trends guide timing of tube removal. Frame pleural drainage as supportive care while upstream pancreatic physiology is addressed with rest, octreotide, and definitive ductal therapy when needed.
